name: Purple toothpaste / colour corrector serum
lead: Purple toothpastes and colour corrector serums are cosmetic dental products, popular in short-video trends, that put a purple pigment on the teeth so they look whiter and less yellow straight away. People use them as a quick, peroxide-free way to brighten a smile before photos or events, and the best-known example is Hismile's V34 Colour Corrector.[3]

The idea is colour theory: violet sits opposite yellow on the colour wheel, so a purple layer is meant to cancel yellow tones,.[1][3] A dentist's blog says the packaging uses the word brightening rather than whitening,[4] and a New Mouth review describes the product as a purple serum that neutralises yellow on contact; the reviewer reported teeth looking a few shades lighter after one use and said the effect is temporary.[3] Peroxide whitening works differently, by oxidising and breaking down pigment molecules.[2]

A dentist's blog post argues the effect comes from a thin, temporary purple stain on the enamel and that the result can look greyish rather than white, while also describing occasional use as relatively harmless.[4] No clinical studies of these products were found.

paras: Products in this category are brushed on or applied as a serum and leave a visible violet film that proponents say offsets yellowish tooth colour.[1][3] A New Mouth review of the V34 lists hydrated silica, a mild abrasive for surface stains, and tetrasodium pyrophosphate, which helps limit tartar and stain build-up, among its ingredients, and reports a price of about $29 for 30 ml.[3]
Dental references note that actual whitening typically uses peroxide agents, with results ranging from one or two shades for home products to more for in-office treatment.[2]

The reviewer describes the serum as drippy, leaving purple marks on lips, skin and towels, and reports applying it occasionally with a soft toothbrush.[3] The dentist's blog describes the product as containing dye but no peroxide bleaching agent.[4]

A dentist writing for his Long Island City practice in 2024 says the product contains no bleaching agent and deposits a thin purple stain that partly neutralises yellow, that it applies mainly to yellower tooth shades, and that the effect washes off with eating, drinking or brushing; he also suggests long-term use could make later peroxide whitening harder. His practice sells a competing peroxide product.[4]

The New Mouth reviewer notes that hydrated silica can wear enamel with hard brushing and that the pyrophosphate ingredient can irritate gums in some customers.[3] Wikipedia's tooth whitening article lists tooth sensitivity and gum irritation as the common side effects of peroxide products, which are a different category.[2]

card.summary: A purple paste or serum that visually offsets yellow teeth; a trend product with no published studies.
card.note: No clinical studies found; effect described as cosmetic.

quick.overview:
Purple toothpaste and colour corrector serums are trend products that tint the teeth so they look less yellow straight away.

No clinical studies were found, so the benefit is based on colour theory and user accounts rather than trials.
quick.mechanism: The purple pigment is said to visually cancel yellow tones, like colour correction in makeup. It does not chemically whiten the tooth.
quick.risks: No published safety data specific to these products were found.

chain: Purple pigment applied to the teeth
Teeth look brighter and less yellow for a short time
angle.text: A purple paste or serum brushed onto the teeth masks yellow tones so the smile looks brighter within minutes. The effect is cosmetic and described by reviewers as temporary.
